item.title: Scaling agentic AI with confidence
item.description:
Your AI agents are making decisions faster than your teams can review them. Governance requires the same speed.

In order to accomplish their given tasks, agents gain access to new applications and business data around the clock. But every autonomous decision raises a question you’ll eventually have to answer: Can you prove the agent acted within policy?

More than half of enterprises are already deploying agentic AI, according to research by Omdia. This growing reliance on AI agents is creating a trust deficit that makes governance and accountability an immediate CIO priority.

Identity governance can help close that deficit by giving CIOs the evidence to demonstrate effective oversight as they expand their use of AI agents.

“Boards are asking CIOs a simple question: can we trust what our AI is doing? Most can’t answer it yet,” said Neil McGlennon, Global Field CTO at SailPoint. “AI has moved from experiment to execution, and closing the trust deficit means knowing which agents exist, what they can access, and who is accountable when they act. Without that, AI stalls at the pilot stage.”

What is audit-ready context?
Boards and auditors expect CIOs to provide clear evidence to back AI agent decisions. This requires context, such as the agent’s identity and human owner, as well as any applications and data involved. The record should also show which policies governed the decision.

This creates a clear line of accountability from the agent’s action back to the person responsible for it. Context needs to be easy to access and understand for non-technical stakeholders.

The case for continuous governance

AI agents rely on a growing number of non-human identities (NHIs) to authenticate and access enterprise resources. These NHIs include machine accounts, API keys, and tokens. Some enterprises have up to 140 NHIs for every employee.

AI agents can quickly change responsibilities and end up retaining permissions they no longer need. This creates unnecessary risk. For example, an agent could keep broad database access after moving from data migration to basic reporting, or keep administrator privileges long after completing a task that required them.

This privilege drift shows why continuous governance matters. Periodic access reviews leave too much time between checks for agents making decisions in real time. Continuous oversight can detect changes in agent behavior and trigger an immediate response, including shutting down an agent when necessary.

The essentials of AI identity governance

Identity and access management (IAM) teams now have AI agents to govern alongside human users. Supporting agentic AI requires three connected capabilities:

  • Discovery and unified visibility
  • Real-time governance and audit
  • Proactive protection and response

Organizations need visibility into the agents and NHIs operating across the enterprise. Governance provides the controls and evidence to oversee their activity, and real-time protection helps teams detect problems and respond immediately.

Keeping AI accountable

AI agents will continue to take on more responsibility across the enterprise, increasing the need for strong identity governance. With the right oversight, CIOs can support broader AI adoption while maintaining accountability for how agents act and what they gain access to.


Explore how CIOs can close the AI trust deficit as agentic AI adoption grows.

item.title: The AI trust deficit: Why explainability, not more automation, is the CIO’s next priority
item.description:
An AI trust deficit occurs when an organization deploys autonomous AI agents faster than it can prove those agents are acting within policy. It’s the gap between what AI agents are doing and what CIOs can clearly explain to a board, auditor, or regulator. Closing that gap requires audit-ready context: evidence showing who owns an agent, what it can access, and which policies governed its decisions.

This gap is widening quickly. More than half of enterprises are already deploying agentic AI, according to Omdia research, and these agents now onboard applications, resolve access requests, and act on business data around the clock. The question is no longer whether AI can move fast. It’s whether you can prove, at any moment, that it moved correctly.

Why the AI trust deficit is a board-level problem

Enterprises want the speed and efficiency that autonomous AI delivers, but speed without accountability creates exposure. When an AI agent makes a decision that no one can trace back to a policy or a person, you don’t have a governance program. You have a liability waiting to surface during your next audit.

The scale of non-human identity has made the issue more urgent. Some enterprises now manage roughly 45 machine identities for every employee, and 67% of enterprise leaders say they’re concerned about the security risk those identities pose. AI agents rely on this same population of API keys, tokens, and service accounts to authenticate and act, which means every new agent amplifies an already sprawling attack surface.

“AI innovation has outpaced AI safety,” says Mike Kiser, director of Strategy and Standards at SailPoint. “The more this gap stretches, the more likely it is that organizations become ticking time bombs just waiting for an incident to happen.”

What audit-ready context actually looks like

Audit-ready context means every AI-driven decision comes with a traceable record, not a black-box outcome. Boards and regulators increasingly expect CIOs to explain not just what an agent did, but why it did it and who is accountable for it.

A defensible answer connects three things every time:

  • Ownership: A named human is responsible for every non-human identity, from creation through retirement.
  • Policy rationale: The specific rule or condition that triggered the agent’s action, tied to a clear business need.
  • Risk evidence: A logged risk score, timestamp, and outcome that justified automation or escalation.

Picture a board asking why a finance access agent approved a request. A CIO with audit-ready context can answer immediately: the agent is owned by the director of financial reporting, the decision followed a specific quarterly access policy, and the action was logged and continuously monitored for behavioral drift. That’s the difference between an explanation and a guess.

Why governance has to be continuous, not periodic

AI agents, business processes, and policies continue to evolve, which means governance has to keep pace or it quickly falls behind. An agent built for one task can retain broad privileges long after its role changes, accumulating access it no longer needs.

Consider how quickly this drift happens in practice:

  • An agent provisioned for temporary data migration keeps its original database privileges after being reassigned to simple reporting.
  • A service desk agent granted administrator-level permissions during a training phase continues running with those privileges long after training ends.
  • A low-privilege chatbot is manipulated through indirect prompt injection into triggering a high-privilege agent that executes unauthorized changes at machine speed.

Periodic reviews can’t catch this kind of drift in time. An agent operating between review cycles can take thousands of actions before anyone notices something went wrong. This is why continuous identity governance, validating access and behavior in real time rather than on a quarterly schedule, has become the baseline expectation, not an enhancement.

Building the foundation for trusted AI

Closing the AI trust deficit starts with treating AI agents the same way you’d treat any privileged digital worker: authenticate every action, authorize every decision, and keep a record of both.

This is where adaptive identity earns its place in the conversation. Rather than relying on static permissions, it adjusts access dynamically as an agent’s role, risk profile, or behavior changes, while still generating the audit trail boards expect. Non-human identity governance extends this same discipline to the machine accounts, tokens, and service identities that agents depend on, ensuring that nothing operates outside your visibility.

A unified platform makes this practical at scale. When identity, access, and policy data live in one control plane rather than scattered across disconnected tools, you can trace a single decision from the moment an agent requests access to the moment that access is approved, denied, or revoked, without stitching together logs from multiple systems after the fact.

Get ahead of the questions your board will ask

Your board and auditors will eventually ask how you’re governing AI, who’s accountable for it, and what evidence proves your safeguards are working. The organizations that answer confidently are the ones that built audit-ready context into their identity program before they needed it.

Download “Closing the AI trust deficit” to learn what explainable AI governance requires and how to build the evidence trail your board will expect.

Then put that knowledge to work with “The CIO agentic AI governance checklist,” a practical two-page assessment for identifying gaps in your AI governance readiness before they become audit findings.

item.title: Governing the agent workforce: New data on the next frontier of AI risk
item.description:
In the fast-paced world of agentic AI, building agents and defending ROI is yesterday’s news. Today, the more pressing challenge is managing and governing the exploding workforce of agents to mitigate growing enterprise risk.

The problem intensifies as AI agents move from advisory to more active roles. According to a survey of 200 IT and AI decision makers conducted by Foundry and Rubrik, most agents are allowed to act with full (26%) or limited (35%) autonomy.

With access to enterprise systems and authority to execute end-to-end tasks, governance, guardrails, and compliance have become key obstacles to AI agent implementation. This was cited by 42% of survey respondents, along with AI agent management, at 18%. Almost one quarter of respondents (24%) cited security and governance as the biggest barrier to their ability to scale agents, even over technical complexities (17%) and lack of proven ROI (14%).

Rubrik

The reality is traditional security, monitoring, and governance solutions are architected to manage human identities, not agentic AI. “We spent decades mastering how to manage humans and we’ve gotten pretty good at that,” says Michael Ortega, Director of AI Marketing at Rubrik. “We don’t yet have that same rigor for agents.”

For example, there is no scenario where a company would hire 1,000 new employees without onboarding or managerial oversight. Nor would they give them access to highly sensitive data right off the bat. “[AI agents] are our new employees, but that’s exactly how we are treating them,” Ortega cautions.

A new governance paradigm

Traditional security and governance guardrails don’t translate well to an agent workforce that moves at machine speed to evaluate and execute thousands of decision points in seconds. AI agents are also probabilistic, which lets them make complex decisions, but also act in unpredictable ways. As a result, a rogue agent can do 10x the damage of a human in one-tenth the time.

Currently, most organizations use logs and manual review or legacy observability platforms to keep tabs on agents. But they lack the holistic visibility and context needed to effectively track agent identity, actions, and downstream impact. There are also a variety of methods employed to govern agents, many paper-based, with limited ability to control agent behavior at run-time.

Without a new paradigm for controls and visibility, AI agents become a vector for significant enterprise risks while undermining business value. Nearly half of survey respondents have had to deal with an agent or chatbot conveying false or incorrect information. Another 38% confirm agents have exfiltrated data or caused a sensitive data leak.

But it’s not because AI agents are inherently malicious – it’s because they lack the common sense of their human counterparts. “We can’t put a human in the loop for everything because that would slow things down,” Ortega explains. “We have to enable our teams to have autonomous workflows without having a human check everything.”

A new breed of solutions is emerging to manage the autonomous workforce. As an example, Rubrik tackles this head-on by leveraging AI to govern AI. Rather than relying on static rules and legacy pattern matching, Rubrik Agent Cloud evaluates real-time behavior anchored in deep data and identity context. Armed with this context, the platform assesses agent intent to block or permit actions before execution. By unifying monitoring, control, and remediation into a single pane of glass, Rubrik delivers holistic visibility across the entire agent estate. For the inevitable moment an AI agent strays, Rubrik’s Rewind initiates granular rollbacks to restore the environment to a known good state, eliminating downtime and data loss.

AI is forcing IT and security leaders to reimagine governance, and platforms that safely unleash the agent workforce are essential for success. See all the insights from the survey on agentic governance and risk.

item.title: When your AI vendor goes belly up
item.description:
With hundreds of AI-related companies increasingly crowding the market for enterprise dollars, IT leaders should prepare for the day when at least one of their AI vendors suddenly shutters or gets acquired.

While the AI market overall is showing few signs of slowing down, a shakeout will eventually happen — with potentially significant ramifications for CIOs. IT leaders only need to be reminded of Broadcom’s acquisition of virtualization giant VMware to visualize what could be at stake.

CIOs, of course, are not unfamiliar with the many issues that arise when an IT vendor shuts down or is acquired. However, suddenly losing an AI vendor creates some special challenges, according to industry experts, including data access and privacy concerns and the loss of AI models trained for specific customer needs.

“Assume your AI vendor will get bought or go under, and plan for it now,” says Dave Shanker, cofounder and managing partner at IT consulting firm STS Consulting Group. “Hundreds of these companies launched in three years, and most won’t last. The ones that do will get acquired, and then pricing, terms, and roadmaps can change overnight.”

Set your exit strategy up front

For now, the demand for AI products seems to be moving ahead at full steam. In May, Gartner projected that the worldwide AI market would grow by 47% in 2026, totaling nearly $2.6 trillion.

But many insiders, including Amazon founder and CEO Jeff Bezos and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have projected that the AI bubble will eventually burst, with many AI startups buried in the rubble.

One warning sign came in mid-October, when consumer-focused Character.AI filed for bankruptcy, with the startup agreeing to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million.

With many vendors likely to go extinct in a few years, it’s incumbent on CIOs to plan ahead for potential market disruptions, Shanker says.

He recommends that IT leaders ensure that their organizations own the data they’re putting into AI models. The organization’s prompts, outputs, fine-tuning data, and anything it has loaded into an AI tool should be exportable in a usable format.

In addition, IT leaders should write the potential exit from an AI vendor into the contract from day one, with notice periods, data return and deletion terms, and the right to leave without a penalty if the vendor is acquired built into the deal.

“Procurement should build this into every contract, AI vendor or not,” he adds. “If they aren’t, that’s a big risk they’re missing.”

IT leaders should also weigh portability against cost, he says. “Sometimes it makes sense to build tightly on one platform, because adding a layer that keeps you portable can double or triple what it costs to run,” he explains. “Redo the analysis at least once a year. Something that’s easy to move today can, after three years of heavy development, leave you stuck.”

AI-specific concerns complicate traditional vendor risk

Rodion Sorokin, CTO of deep-tech venture studio The Capital Index, agrees that CIOs need to prepare for an eventual market shakeup. Sorokin points to information from company shutdown assistance provider SimpleClosure, which noted that AI companies are currently a small and shrinking percentage of the types of closures they handle.

However, the median age at closure is lower for AI companies: 2.30 years versus 3.78 for other companies, according to SimpleClosure. 

“We hypothesize that the 2023-2025 AI cohort is still in its early days, and we’re only beginning to see how it plays out,” SimpleClosure CEO Dori Yona wrote in a blog post,

Even if the early warning signs are few and far between, CIOs should be prepared to quickly switch vendors, Sorokin says. Not only should IT leaders be able to export prompts, outputs, logs, fine-tuning data, and other information in usable formats as STS Consulting’s Shanker advises, but they should also test those processes before they sign a contract with any AI vendor, he recommends.

“Assume every AI vendor will be acquired or shut down within your contract term, and negotiate for that day,” he says.

CIOs should also be aware of specific concerns that pertain to the sudden loss of an AI vendor, Sorokin says. For example, their organization’s data and customizations may live within the vendor’s product, and it’s possible all that gets deleted if the vendor goes under or is acquired, he notes.

In addition, switching AI tools can render AI-aided workflows suddenly inoperable, he says.

“Switching isn’t a migration; it’s a revalidation,” Sorokin says. “A new model behaves differently on the same prompts, so every workflow has to be retested. Without your own evaluation suite, you can’t switch safely.”

CIOs should also know that notice can be measured in days, he adds. In June 2025, Anthropic cut Windsurf’s direct access to its Claude models with less than five days of notice, amid reports of an OpenAI acquisition of the smaller company.

While some observers say there may be safety in going with the big players in the AI space, others suggest startups may offer services that aren’t available from the big boys. In addition, large AI vendors have also cancelled services on short notice, Sorokin notes, with OpenAI shutting down its Sora app in April and the Sora API in September.

“Size helps, but it isn’t continuity,” he says. “Choose portability over logos: an open-weight model you can run yourself as a fallback, and contracts that guarantee export.”

IT leaders exploring options

While signs of a busting bubble are hard to find, many IT leaders are preparing for the future, says Colin Woods, CEO and co-founder of high-performance infrastructure provider FreedomTechSolutions.

A growing number of IT leaders are beginning to reassess the level of dependency they are willing to place on AI platforms and cloud-hosted services, he notes.

“From our perspective, concerns around AI vendor consolidation are already influencing customer decision-making,” Woods explains. “While the rapid growth of the AI market has driven innovation, it has also created a crowded ecosystem of providers, many of whom face uncertain long-term viability.”

In some cases, IT leaders are moving away from hyperscalers for certain AI workloads, with a renewed focus on infrastructure ownership, data sovereignty, and operational control, he says.

“Organizations are increasingly concerned about where their data resides, how it is processed, and what happens if a vendor is acquired, changes its commercial model, or discontinues a service altogether,” he adds. “For many businesses, AI is becoming too strategic a capability to be entirely dependent on an external provider whose roadmap they do not control.”

Some organizations are deploying smaller, dedicated AI environments in regional or edge data centers, Woods says. “These AI nodes allow organizations to run inference and specialized workloads closer to their data, while retaining full governance over models, datasets, and infrastructure,” he adds.

item.title: Cadence Maestro puts domain-trained AI agents to work for chip design
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has been part of semiconductor design for years, helping engineers optimize chip architectures for performance, power efficiency, silicon area and faster development. More recently, the industry has begun integrating large language models and AI agents into established electronic design automation (EDA) workflows. Now Cadence Design Systems is taking that approach further with its Maestro AI Model Portfolio, a collection of domain-specialized models designed to work with the company’s engineering software and AI Super Agents.

Maestro combines specialized model training, reinforcement learning and established EDA tools to improve how AI agents execute engineering tasks and evaluate results. Cadence claims better design outcomes with greater token efficiency versus general-purpose foundation models. While initially focused on chip and electronic system design, I also see broader implications for enterprise AI economics, proprietary data protection and deployment across complex engineering and business applications.

AI builds on established engineering software

Modern semiconductor design is enormously complex. Engineers must balance performance, power consumption, silicon area, manufacturing constraints and costs across chips containing billions of transistors. Cadence and chief competitor Synopsys have spent decades developing software to optimize for these challenges, and both are now incorporating AI agents capable of executing increasingly complex engineering workflows using those tools.

Cadence Design Systems, Inc.

“Revolutionizing complex engineering tasks requires deep domain-specialized intelligence,” notes Cadence president and CEO Anirudh Devgan in the company’s announcement. In my discussions with Cadence executives, we explored how Maestro builds on that approach to improve engineering workflows and design outcomes.

Cadence Maestro combines domain-specialized, post-trained language models, trained decision models and reusable agent skills with Cadence’s EDA and system design automation (SDA) tools. The portfolio supports ChipStack, InnoStack, ViraStack and AuraStack AI Super Agents, which interpret engineering objectives, break them into tasks and engage appropriate models and software tools. Rather than relying on a single model, agents can combine Maestro with commercial frontier and open-weight models according to workload requirements.

What I find particularly interesting is Cadence’s reinforcement learning architecture. EDA tools, evaluation frameworks and deterministic solvers assess AI-generated outputs against engineering constraints, including timing, power and physical design requirements. That feedback can improve subsequent model decisions and agent behavior. It’s a potentially important advantage over relying exclusively on general-purpose LLMs, since engineering results can be evaluated against measurable design constraints rather than language-based assessments alone.

NVIDIA is contributing its Nemotron model technology and collaborating with Cadence on agent security through its OpenShell AI sandboxing architecture, with integration work by both companies underway.

The business case for domain-trained AI in engineering

Cadence Design Systems, Inc.

Cadence reports that initial Maestro evaluations delivered up to 30% better quality of results and five times greater token efficiency, compared to a general-purpose foundation model. These are early vendor-reported results, however, and Cadence hasn’t disclosed enough benchmark detail to establish how consistently those advantages translate across production workloads.

Greater token efficiency is always a goal of course, particularly for AI agents executing lengthy, iterative engineering tasks. But reducing token consumption doesn’t always translate into proportional cost reductions. Engineering software, simulation infrastructure, verification and available compute resources also contribute substantially to development costs.

To me, the larger opportunity is improving design quality and shortening development cycles. Chip development programs can require hundreds of engineers and substantial capital investment, so even modest productivity improvements or faster time to market can offer significant value.

Cadence Design Systems, Inc.

Cadence customer Socionext expects up to fivefold productivity gains from deploying the company’s InnoStack AI Super Agent in production, although that’s a projection rather than a demonstrated Maestro result. Silicon Labs has also reported faster root-cause analysis and debugging using Cadence’s ChipStack technology. These examples show progress with agent-based engineering, but Maestro’s performance claims still need production validation. I’ll be interested to see how those results develop.

Deployment flexibility and data control

Another noteworthy aspect of Maestro is deployment flexibility. Cadence says its agentic engineering environment supports deployment through its own secure cloud platform, supported public clouds or customer-controlled on-prem infrastructure. Customers can also further train supported models using proprietary engineering data.

For semiconductor companies, where intellectual property can represent billions of dollars in investment, maintaining control over sensitive design information is critical. Similar considerations apply in financial services, healthcare and aerospace, where proprietary data and regulatory requirements can complicate AI deployment.

The tradeoffs warrant examination, however. On-prem deployments can shift responsibility for GPU infrastructure, model updates, security controls and optimization to the customer. Those costs need to be weighed against cloud inference expenses, data residency requirements and the potential performance benefits of processing data close to engineering workloads. In my view, Cadence’s deployment flexibility is valuable because enterprises can evaluate these choices against their infrastructure, security policies and engineering economics.

Specialized AI continues to gain momentum in chip design

Cadence Maestro is part of a broader industry push toward AI-driven semiconductor engineering. Established EDA vendors are expanding their agentic capabilities, while AI-native startups are developing systems for RTL generation, verification, debugging and physical design optimization. Domain-trained models, engineering feedback loops and intelligent model routing are also gaining attention.

What’s interesting here is the potential for agents to coordinate multiple engineering tools and models while retaining the design context needed for complex tasks. The business opportunity extends beyond automating individual steps to reducing the effort required to reach verified design results. For enterprise technology execs, that puts greater emphasis on toolchain integration, measurable productivity improvements and the economics of AI-assisted engineering.

Proving the value of specialized AI in chip design

Cadence’s first Maestro models are entering select customer early access in the fourth quarter of 2026, so it’s too early to know whether the company’s performance claims will translate consistently into production.

General-purpose models will remain important for broad reasoning, language and multimodal applications. However, specialized engineering processes often demand deeper domain knowledge, validated results and tight integration with existing software.

From my perspective, Cadence’s approach offers a glimpse of where enterprise AI is heading. Selecting the right models, tools and deployment architecture for specific workloads will be critical as adoption expands. And the early results are promising, with specialized AI showing the potential to improve engineering outcomes, boost productivity and reduce development costs at scale.

item.title: The moat is dry – Part 2: A roadmap for rebuilding
item.description:
In Part 1 of this two-part series, I argued that the moat is dry. When NotPetya hit Merck in 2017, it didn’t climb a wall. It came in through trusted vendor software, the routine traffic every perimeter is built to admit, and Merck put the damage at more than $1.4 billion. Its insurers then tried not to pay, and after that fight, underwriters started asking much harder questions.

AI has since made attacks like that cheaper and faster. In IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach report, one in four malicious breaches was AI-enabled, and breaches that took more than 200 days to find and contain cost about $1.3 million more than those that didn’t. Deepfaked executives, software that can be talked into things and AI agents holding credentials are attacks on trust first and technology second.

Yet the people we hold responsible are set up to lose. Some 64% of CISOs still report into IT leadership, only 10% influence financial decisions, and only a quarter say board discussions of cyber risk run longer than 30 minutes. They are accountable for the breach without budget authority, and they check the work of the people they report to.

The organizations that feel safest about the next two years are not the ones with the most tools. They are the ones where leadership understands AI risk, someone clearly owns it, and the security team has the authority to act. That is a governance problem, and it has a governance fix.

A roadmap for reconstruction

1. Take security out of IT, and do it before the breach

No company lets the finance department audit its own books. That is why internal audit reports to the board’s audit committee rather than to the CFO. Security deserves the same independence for the same reason: the people who build and run the systems should not vouch for them. The CISO’s job is not to run technology. It is to govern how people, partners and machines behave around the things the organization cannot afford to lose, and to tell leadership the truth about that risk.

That does not make the job less technical. A CISO who can’t read an architecture diagram, question an engineer or spot a vendor’s overstatement will be steamrolled in the first meeting. The role needs an engineer’s depth. It is just bigger than engineering, the way a general counsel needs to know the law but is hired for judgment.

In practice, that means a direct line to the CEO and a board committee. Equifax did this after its 2017 breach. Its new CISO, Jamil Farshchi, called the direct line to the CEO and board the key to the turnaround, and noted that it costs nothing. Vertex Pharmaceuticals took a different route: its CISO reports to the Chief Scientific Officer, which puts security next to what the company actually protects, its research. Choose a model deliberately. Most organizations never choose; they inherit one.

2. Hand the CISO the AI governance pen

Only 19% of organizations report coordination between their AI governance and security teams. Every AI tool the business adopts is a security design decision, and it needs one accountable owner. Otherwise, you have a committee that approves tools and a security team that finds out later. But accountable doesn’t mean alone, which brings us to the most important step.

3. Give everyone a voice

A CISO knows security. A CISO does not know research, or claims processing, or the manufacturing line. Elevating the CISO works only if decisions get made with the people who live with them: research leaders, business owners, legal, finance and the CIO. Build a standing risk council where those voices shape controls before they’re imposed, and where a scientist can say “this will break my work” and be taken seriously. The point of elevating the CISO isn’t to put one person in charge of everyone else’s work. It’s to make sure the person who owns the risk is in the room, and that everyone affected by the decision is in the room too.

Security decisions made in isolation get worked around. Decisions made together get followed.

4. Define “ready,” then hire and develop to it

New York’s cybersecurity regulation for financial firms calls the CISO “a qualified individual” but never says what qualified means. Here’s a working definition, in the form of two tests a board can give. The first is technical, and it is not optional:

  • Can you tell us what we own, who can reach it, and how fast we can recover, and when did we last test that?
  • Have you personally used the AI tools our employees use? Can you explain prompt injection and agent permissions to us in plain English?
  • Where does your threat knowledge come from besides vendors: peer networks, industry information-sharing groups, red-team results?

The second test is about judgment and behavior. It is the one most security leaders are never given:

  • What do our people actually do when a request seems urgent and comes from someone senior?
  • Which risks have you advised us to accept, and why? A CISO who never recommends accepting a risk is a gatekeeper, not a risk officer.
  • Can you translate a risk into dollars and days of downtime?
  • Which research and business leaders do you consult before a control changes how they work?

And one question for the board itself: Have we given this person authority that matches their accountability?

👉 Click here to download a sample CISO job description👈

5. Make sure AI agents are governed like employees

The CISO doesn’t provision these accounts; the CISO makes sure someone is accountable for every one of them. Every non-human identity needs an owner, the least privilege it needs, monitoring, and a kill switch. Among organizations that had an AI-related incident, 92% lacked proper AI access controls.

6. Hold everyone to the clock, not the checklist

Ask every part of the organization for time to detect, time to contain and time to recover, using tested numbers rather than estimates, and report them to the board. The 200-day line in IBM’s data is worth more than a million dollars per breach.

7. Make sure the boring things get done

Encryption, multi-factor authentication, asset inventory and network segmentation are not glamorous, but they are exactly what insurers began requiring after the Merck case. Doing this work belongs to the technology teams. The CISO’s job is to verify that it’s done and to tell the board plainly when it isn’t. If your underwriter is asking for these controls, your board should be too.

8. Give the board more than 30 minutes

Make cyber a budget conversation rather than a status update. If the CISO’s board time is spent on regulatory trends instead of business trade-offs, the board is being briefed, not governed.

A word to CIOs

I know how this reads to a CIO: someone telling you to give up a direct report. But a CISO who reports to the CIO is grading the boss’s homework. The CIO is measured on availability and speed of delivery. The CISO is measured on risk. That tension is healthy only between peers. Elevating the CISO doesn’t diminish the CIO; it frees the CIO to build without also serving as auditor of what they built. The two roles aren’t a senior and a junior version of the same job. One builds and runs the organization’s technology. The other is responsible for whether the organization, its people included, can be trusted.

A good CIO should lean on the CISO and also be a little afraid of the CISO, the way a good CFO relies on the auditor and is a little afraid of what the auditor will find. That fear is not hostility; it is the reason the books stay clean. Pair it with the partnership described above, and the CIO gets something no direct report can offer: someone with the standing to say “no, not like that” before the board has to hear it from an attacker.

The CIO’s seat at the table appeared when technology became the business. The CISO’s is appearing because trust has become the business, and AI has made that impossible to ignore. Some organizations are already moving. In IBM’s follow-on research, 85% said they plan to increase security spending after learning what frontier AI models can do to their systems, compared with 64% who planned to spend more after suffering a breach. Learning from the threat is far cheaper than learning from the post-mortem, and the organizations that get there first will be the ones where security, research and the business decide together.

The moat is dry. Stop dredging it, and give the person defending the castle a seat at the table.

item.title: The moat is dry – Part 1: Why the old security model failed
item.description:
In June 2017, a piece of malware called NotPetya got into Merck & Co. without climbing a single wall. It arrived through a backdoor in accounting software supplied by a Ukrainian vendor, the kind of trusted, routine traffic every perimeter is built to let through. It spread to some 40,000 of the drugmaker’s computers, and Merck put the damage at more than $1.4 billion.

Then several of Merck’s insurers argued they owed nothing, because the attack was attributed to Russian military intelligence and their policies excluded acts of war. The fight ended in a confidential settlement in January 2024.

Two lessons sit in that story. The moat didn’t matter, because the threat came in with the traffic the moat was designed to admit. And the people who price risk for a living were the first to notice and the first to send the bill.

That was 2017, when attackers still needed humans at the keyboard. Increasingly, they don’t.

Here is the argument of this two-part series in two sentences. Security stopped being a technology problem with business consequences; it is now a business risk with a technology component. Most organizations are still organized the other way around, and the person they hold responsible for that risk sits inside the IT department, reporting to the people whose work they are supposed to check.

What AI actually changed

IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report, based on 602 breached organizations, found that one in four malicious breaches was AI-enabled, a 56% jump in a single year. Those breaches averaged $6 million, about $1 million above the global average of $4.99 million. In the U.S., the average breach now costs $11.5 million.

You don’t need a computer science degree to understand what changed. Three things matter:

  • The con got a better voice. Deepfake impersonation was the most common AI-driven attack in IBM’s data, at 45%. The oldest scam in business, the urgent wire transfer, now arrives in the CFO’s actual voice on a video call.
  • Your software can be talked into things. “Prompt injection” means hiding instructions inside an email, document or web page that an AI assistant reads and then obeys. It is social engineering aimed at the software instead of the employee, and no amount of annual phishing training protects against it.
  • You’ve hired employees with no background check. Every AI agent holding credentials is, in effect, a new hire with keys to your systems, no manager and no HR file.

Notice what those three have in common. Each one is an attack on trust, on whom we believe, what we obey and whom we let in, and only then on technology. That distinction matters for everything that follows.

Meanwhile, employees aren’t waiting for permission. Shadow AI, meaning tools staff use without sanction, showed up in 43% of breached organizations this year, up from 20% the year before. Breaches involving AI systems themselves rose to 21% of all incidents, and the most common way in wasn’t the model at all. It was the plumbing around it: compromised APIs and plug-ins, and misconfigured cloud workloads.

Why the moat is dry

Moat security is easy to recognize. There’s a perimeter, a couple of expensive appliances, an annual training module, and a binder of procedures nobody reads until the auditor visits. It assumes the enemy is outside.

Today, much of the risk has been invited in the assistant reading the email, the agent holding the credentials, the vendor pushing the update. When Johnson Controls was hit by ransomware in 2023, the attackers first got into the company’s Asia offices and spread from there across the network. The company confirmed data theft and more than $27 million in costs, net of insurance. One breach in a distant office, and the moat was irrelevant.

Moat organizations measure activity. Attackers measure time. IBM found the average time to identify and contain a breach rose to 247 days, the first increase in five years. Breaches contained in under 200 days cost $4.32 million; those that ran longer cost $5.65 million. And 53% of breached organizations hadn’t encrypted sensitive data at rest and in transit. The basics still aren’t done.

My email signature reads “Process is the evil twin of progress.” Moat security is process mistaken for protection.

Prepared versus old school: the numbers

In fairness, IBM sells security tools, and I’m aware of the irony of citing a vendor in a piece that warns against learning from vendors. The fieldwork is done by the Ponemon Institute, though, and the pattern matches what independent CISO surveys show. The gap between prepared and unprepared organizations is not subtle:

Sources: IBM/Ponemon, Cost of a Data Breach 2026; IANS/Artico Search, CISO Perspectives on AI Risk 2026.

The most revealing finding comes from the IANS survey of 113 CISOs. Mature AI security programs explained why some security chiefs feel safer today. But confidence about the next two years tracked something else: whether leadership understood AI risk, whether someone clearly owned AI governance, and whether the security team had budget authority and enough staff. In other words, the factor that matters most is governance, not technology.

The CISO problem: under-trained and under-armed

Under-trained. Many of today’s security leaders learned the job defending against people, not software that behaves like people, and much of what they know about AI came from the companies selling the cure. When IANS released its research this year, one of its partners pointed out that most AI risk data comes from vendors and so reflects the supply side. If your threat briefings, your training and your tools all come from the same sales channel, you’ll end up with a well-funded blind spot. Only 53% of CISOs in a LevelBlue survey said they felt prepared to defend against AI-enabled adversaries.

This is not about age. A veteran who keeps learning beats a newly certified buyer of AI-branded appliances every time. What matters is whether someone is still learning now, not when they first learned.

Under-armed. The IANS 2026 board engagement study found that 95% of CISOs brief their boards regularly, but only 10% influence financial decisions. Only a quarter say board discussions of cyber risk run longer than 30 minutes. And 64% of CISOs still report into IT leadership. That leaves the CISO accountable for the breach without authority over the budget.

The lab is not the accounting department

Everything above gets harder in a research organization. Research runs on unpredictable workflows, tools adopted the week they appear, enormous data transfers and outside collaborators. A control that slows a scientist doesn’t stop the work. It moves the work somewhere security can’t see.

The stakes are rising at the same time. Google’s threat intelligence group reported that in the second quarter of this year it investigated extortion cases involving stolen AI research, including one in which a healthcare organization lost drug research and an AI model. It also tracked a China-linked group targeting academic, medical and military research institutions in North America.

R&D doesn’t need an exemption. It needs a different deal: wide freedom in how the work gets done, in exchange for a short list of fixed rules around the assets that matter most. In practice, that means protecting around the lab rather than inside it:

  • Make the safe path the fast path. Offer pre-approved sandboxes, compute environments and AI tools that are quicker to use than the workarounds. Researchers don’t resist security; they resist friction.
  • Watch instead of block. Monitor what leaves the lab and how, rather than putting a checkpoint in front of every action. Unusual data movement and odd access patterns are how theft gets caught without slowing discovery.
  • Classify by value, not by department. Open science, pre-publication results and proprietary or controlled work need different protection. Lock down the crown jewels, not the whole lab.
  • Borrow from the research networks. The research and education networking community solved a version of this years ago with the Science DMZ, a design that moves high-performance research traffic outside the enterprise firewall and secures it with targeted controls and monitoring instead.

Some rules don’t bend: federal research-security requirements, defense contracting standards, export controls. But that list should be short, explicit and explained, not a binder of procedures nobody in the lab can name.

We regulate security by tax status, not consequence

Public companies must describe board oversight of cyber risk to the SEC, though the final rule dropped a proposal to disclose whether they even have a CISO. New York’s financial regulator requires the CISO to report to the board in writing every year, and the board must understand and fund the program, public or private. Hospitals still operate under a HIPAA Security Rule written in 2003; its overhaul has slipped to July 2027. A privately held research firm can fail as badly as any public company, and the rules barely notice. Don’t wait for a regulator to tell you what your risk already has.

That is the diagnosis. In Part 2, the prescription: an eight-step roadmap for rebuilding, starting with the reporting line that most organizations never chose and simply inherited.

item.title: OffSec Launches Free PHP2Shell Lab Following Critical Vulnerability Discovery
item.description:
New hands-on lab lets security practitioners explore PHP2Shell exploitation firsthand as AI-assisted research reshapes vulnerability discovery.

OffSec today announced the release of a free, interactive hands-on lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play) to help security practitioners examine and defend against the critical “PHP2Shell” vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) firsthand. Developed in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and active exploits targeting core PHP engines in the wild, the lab provides penetration testers and enterprise defenders with a safe, controlled environment to study the decade-old memory corruption flaws and implement timely server mitigations.

The two critical flaws sat inside PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, for more than a decade. Then researchers at Wiz, a Google-owned cloud security company, pointed AI at the code. 

They found the first flaw Aug. 19. The next day they used it to take over a Drupal site without a password. The day after that, it worked on WordPress.

PHP disclosed the flaws Oct. 21 as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. An attacker with no login can send a series of crafted web requests to crash a server or take it over. PHP’s severity scores rate both vulnerabilities as complex to exploit, even though working attacks already existed. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends patching immediately. 

Attackers are moving fast. Amazon calls PHP2Shell broadly exploited in the wild. By Oct.24, researchers had confirmed attackers running commands on vulnerable honeypot servers. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Oct. 26. 

“PHP is one of those technologies attackers love to see,” said Keegan Bowen, principal DevOps lead at OffSec. “It has been a great attack vector over the years with many exploits and potential abuses. PHP wasn’t designed with security from the start.”

OffSec, which has taught hands-on offensive security since 2006, has released a free PHP2Shell lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play). The lab gives penetration testers and other security professionals a controlled environment to explore CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 firsthand. OffSec’s blog breaks down both flaws, and its proof-of-concept exploit is available on Exploit-DB. 

AI and the Evolving Pace of Exploitation

PHP scored both flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. To build a working attack, Wiz researchers had to chain several bugs together and tune the attack to each server’s memory. When they let AI do the grind, one researcher finished in a week what once took a top team month. Attackers can use the same AI models, so flaws once ranked too complex to matter are now fair game. 

“At this point, attackers are heavily leaning on AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities; the rate of CVEs is roughly double what was reported last year,” said Matt Freitas-Stavola, staff software engineer at OffSec. “LLMs don’t get tired and can easily run in the background for as long as attackers have money or compute to spare. Even now, just a hint of where an issue could arise is enough for an LLM to get a workable POC out relatively quickly.”

The Effects of These Flaws

Both flaws start with the same weak spot: what PHP does when a request runs out of memory or hits another fatal error.

“PHP is built from C and memory management becomes increasingly challenging as the code grows,” Bowen said. “Some out-of-memory states were not handled well. In some cases, attackers can access interrupted state data before it is cleaned up. That becomes an opportunity for abuse.”

That leftover state can carry into the next request on the same worker. An attacker who shapes it can run code with the web server’s privileges.

The same bugs can also leak data. Wiz showed attackers could potentially read memory from the PHP process. That memory could hold passwords, session tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests or the server itself. 

The story is still developing. On Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that can affect fully patched servers with an unusual session setup. PHP has no fix for it yet. Researchers have also built PHP2Shell exploits that get past ASLR, a common memory defense, and more issues could surface as the flaws are studied. As research continues, new vulnerabilities, exploitation techniques, and mitigations may emerge beyond those covered here.

OffSec’s Current Recommendations

These steps reflect what is known at the time of publication. Check CISA and the PHP project for the latest recommendations.

  • Patch PHP Now. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Check vendor advisories rather than relying on version numbers alone.
  • Update the Underlying PHP Engine. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or another application does not resolve vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Rebuild affected container images, and restart PHP processes so the updated code takes effect.
  • Apply Temporary Protections While Patching. Disable PHP session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0), which also mitigates CVE-2026-115560. On PHP 8.5, disable fatal error backtraces and restart affected workers after configuration changes. These measures reduce exposure; they do not replace patching.
  • Investigate Potential Compromise. Review web server and PHP logs for suspicious multipart requests, memory-limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, malformed session cookies, and unexpected PHP worker restarts. Investigations should consider activity dating back to at least October 17, when exploitation attempts were first reported. Rotate potentially affected credentials, API keys, and tokens as appropriate.

Understand the Exploit. Strengthen the Defense.

When the next disclosure lands, someone on the team needs to judge exposure. Reading about an exploit builds awareness. Working on one hands-on builds the skill to respond. 

OffSec’s PHP2Shell lab helps practitioners turn technical knowledge into hands-on experience they can apply to future vulnerabilities. For a deeper look at the vulnerabilities, explore OffSec’s technical analysis. Organizations looking to build these capabilities across their security teams can explore OffSec’s workforce development programs.
